sentences: The woman is a stressed mother of two living in a city.
Her husband is an aspiring motivational speaker and life coach.
The teenager, the mother's philosopher-admiring teenage son from her previous marriage, has taken a vow of silence until he accomplishes his dream of becoming a fighter pilot.
The mother's older brother, a gay scholar of a novelist, is living with the family after attempting suicide.
The father's foul-mouthed father is also living with the family after being evicted from a retirement home for snorting heroin.
The girl, the father and the mother's 7-year-old daughter, is an aspiring beauty queen coached by the grandfather.
The girl learns she has qualified for a beauty pageant being held in a town in another state, in two days.
The father, the mother, and the grandfather want to support her, and the uncle and the teenager cannot be left alone, so the whole family attends.
Due to financial constraints, they go on an 800-mile (1,300 km) road trip in their yellow van.
Family tensions play out along the way, amidst the aging van's mechanical problems.
When the van's clutch breaks early on, the only way to drive it is to push it fast enough for the driver to put it into third gear, then jump in the open side door.
Later, the van's horn starts honking by itself, and at one point the side door falls off.
Throughout the trip, the family suffer numerous personal setbacks and discover their need for each other's support.
While buying pornography for the grandfather at a gas station, the uncle embarrassingly meets the ex-boyfriend who, in leaving him for an academic rival, had prompted his suicide attempt.
The father loses an important contract with a businessman that would have jump-started his motivational business.
The grandfather snorts heroin in his room, leading to a fatal overdose.
When the hospital staff refuse to let the family leave his corpse behind while they go to the pageant, they smuggle it out the window and into the van's trunk.
They are almost caught when a police officer pulls them over because of the honking horn, only escaping due to the police officer's fascination with the pornography.
During the final leg of the trip, the teenager discovers he is color blind, meaning he cannot become a pilot.
This revelation prompts him to finally break his silence and shout his disdain for his family, though he apologizes after the girl calms him with a gentle hug.
After a frantic race against the clock, the family arrives at the pageant hotel.
The mother prepares the girl for her performance while the father makes arrangements for the grandfather's body.
The other contestants are slim, sexualized pre-teens who perform elaborate dance numbers with great panache.
Fearing that the amateur girl will be humiliated, the father and the teenager try to stop her from performing, but the mother insists that they "let the girl be the girl", and she goes on stage.
The hitherto-unseen dance routine the grandfather had taught the girl is revealed to be a striptease performed to a remix of a singer's song.
The girl is oblivious to the subtext of the routine, but it horrifies and angers most of the audience, and the pageant organizer demands she be removed from the stage.
The father physically prevents this, and the family all join the girl on stage, dancing alongside her to show their support.
The family is later released from the hotel's security office on the condition that the girl never enter a beauty pageant in the state again.
Piling into the van with the horn still honking, they begin their trip home to their city.
In intercut frame stories, two ongoing depositions play out: in one, the programmer is being sued by his former friend, and in the other, he is sued by twins.
On October 28, 2003, the 19-year-old programmer, a university sophomore, is dumped by his girlfriend.
Returning to his dorm, the programmer writes an insulting post about her on his blog.
The programmer creates a campus website by hacking and downloading photos of female students from house face books, then allowing site visitors to rate their attractiveness.
After traffic to the site crashes parts of the university's computer network, the programmer is given six months of academic probation.
The campus website's popularity attracts the attention of the twins and their business partner.
The trio invites the programmer to work on their project, a dating-focused social network exclusive to the university's students.
Soon after, the programmer approaches the friend with an idea for the new site, a social networking website that would be exclusive to elite university students.
As its CFO, the friend provides $1,000 in seed funding so the programmer can build the website, which quickly becomes popular.
When they learn about the new site, the twins and their business partner are incensed, believing the programmer stole their idea and misled them by stalling development on their project.
They raise their complaint with the university president, who dismisses it and sees no value in disciplining the new site or the programmer.
The friend and the programmer meet a fellow student, who asks them to "website me," a phrase that impresses them.
As the new site grows in popularity, the programmer expands the network to three other universities.
The friend begins dating the fellow student, who arranges a meeting between him and the programmer and an entrepreneur, the co-founder of another company.
The entrepreneur presents a "billion-dollar" vision for the company, impressing the programmer.
The friend dismisses the entrepreneur as paranoid and delusional, except for his suggestion to shorten the new site's name.

The friend deposits $18,000 into a new account as the programmer relocates the company to another city on the entrepreneur's advice; the friend remains in a different city to work on business development while breaking up with the fellow student.
The entrepreneur later moves into the house the programmer uses as a base of operations and becomes more involved with the company, much to the friend's annoyance.

After narrowly losing in a 2004 regatta for the university against a rowing club abroad, the twins discover that, through the entrepreneur, the website has expanded overseas with three universities, and decide to sue the company for intellectual property theft.

Meanwhile, the friend objects to the entrepreneur's decision-making at the company and freezes the company's bank account during the dispute, but relents when the programmer reveals that they have secured $500,000 from an angel investor.

The friend is invited to the company's new headquarters in a city on the pretense of attending a business meeting and "millionth user party," but is enraged when he discovers that the new investment deal dilutes his share of the company from 34% to 0.03%, without diluting the ownership percentage of any other owner.
He is also removed from the masthead as co-founder and CFO.
He confronts the programmer and the entrepreneur, vowing to sue as security removes him from the building.
Shortly after, the entrepreneur is apprehended for cocaine possession with a minor at a party celebrating one million users.
He attempts to blame the friend, prompting the programmer to cut ties with him.

A junior lawyer for the programmer tells the programmer they will settle with the friend because the sordid details of the company's founding and the programmer's callous attitude will make him unlikable to a jury.
Alone, the programmer sends his ex-girlfriend a friend request on the site and repeatedly refreshes the page.
Closing text reveals both cases were settled out of court, and the programmer became the world's youngest billionaire.
In a cemetery in a former nation, a young woman visits the shrine of a renowned writer, known simply as "Author", carrying a copy of his bestselling novel.
The book, written in 1985, recounts the author's 1968 visit to the once lavish, then drab hotel during a bout of writer's block.
There he meets its proprietor, who divulges his rags to riches story over dinner.
In 1932, the proprietor flees his war-ravaged country to work as a lobby boy for the philandering concierge at the hotel.
The concierge seduces the hotel's old, wealthy residents, including a dowager, with whom he has had a nearly two-decade affair.
Shortly after her last visit, the concierge learns from the lobby boy that the dowager has mysteriously died.
He and the lobby boy visit her estate to pay their respects; they encounter her surviving relatives at the reading of her will by her attorney.
The attorney announces that she has bequeathed a famous Renaissance painting to the concierge.
The dowager's son is outraged and demands the concierge's arrest.
The concierge and the lobby boy abscond with the painting.
The dowager's butler makes a deposition implicating the concierge in her death.
He goes into hiding and the concierge is arrested on suspicion of murder.
The concierge befriends a gang during his imprisonment, and the men plot their escape.
He has the lobby boy place digging tools inside pastries made by the bakery's apprentice baker, the lobby boy's girlfriend.
The concierge and the others dig their way out and disperse.
The son deploys his hitman.
The hitman, to kill the attorney and the butler's sister, who conceals her brother's whereabouts.
When the lobby boy and the concierge are reunited, they set out to prove the concierge's innocence with the assistance of a fraternity of concierges.
They locate the butler, and a meeting is orchestrated for the three.
The lobby boy and the concierge learn the butler was pressured to frame the concierge by the son to cover up evidence incriminating the son as the true perpetrator of the dowager's murder.
The butler tells them that the dowager had a missing second will which would only become effective if she was murdered.
The hitman arrives and kills the butler, leaving the concierge and the lobby boy without a witness.
After a chase, the concierge dangles off a cliff at the hitman's mercy.
The lobby boy rescues the concierge by pushing the hitman off the cliff, and the two men flee, closely trailed by the country's police.
The concierge, the lobby boy, and the baker arrive at the hotel to find it converted into a military headquarters.
The baker sneaks in to retrieve the painting; as she is leaving, the son enters the hotel and spots her with the painting.
The concierge and the lobby boy rush to save the baker from the son.
He opens fire on them, initiating a melee with the country's troops.
The baker's attempt to escape leaves her and the lobby boy hanging from a balcony before falling, safely, into a van full of pastries.
The dowager's second will, which makes the concierge the beneficiary of her fortune, is found attached to the back of the painting.
The concierge is exonerated in court, after which the son disappears.
The lobby boy takes over as concierge and marries the baker in a ceremony officiated by the concierge.
While traveling by train, the three encounter thuggish soldiers who try to arrest the lobby boy, but the concierge attempts to fend them off and they shoot him dead.
The lobby boy inherits the concierge's fortune and retains the hotel in memory of the baker, who died from the grippe with their infant son.
The man is captured by the hydraulic despot cult leader's warriors and taken to his fortress.
The man, a universal donor, is forced to transfuse his blood to a sick warrior.
Meanwhile, the despot sends his lieutenant in the armoured rig to trade produce and water for petrol and ammunition with two of his allies.
When the despot realises his five "wives" are fleeing in the rig, he leads his entire army in pursuit, calling on his allies to help.
The warrior joins the pursuit with the man strapped to his car, and a chasing battle ensues.

After entering enemy territory and fending off a rival gang, the lieutenant drives into a dust choked supercell and loses all of her pursuers except the warrior, who attempts to sacrifice himself to blow up the rig.
The man frees himself and restrains the warrior, and the lieutenant destroys the warrior's car.
After the sandstorm, the man catches the lieutenant repairing the rig, accompanied by the despot's "wives", two of them being pregnant with the despot's children.
The man fights and subdues the lieutenant, but her engine kill switch prevents him from stealing the rig.
The man begrudgingly agrees to help the lieutenant's group escape the despot's wrath.
The warrior sneaks onto the rig and attempts to kill the lieutenant, but the women overpower him and throw the warrior out.
The warrior rejoins the despot's army when it catches up.
The lieutenant drives through a canyon controlled by a biker gang, having prearranged to trade petrol for safe passage.
The bikers betray her when they spot the despot's army approaching, forcing her to flee.
The bikers detonate the canyon walls to block the despot and pursue the rig as the man and the lieutenant fend them off.
The despot drives over the blockade in a monster truck and catches up with the rig.
He sends the warrior to carjack the rig, but the warrior stumbles and drops his weapon, to the despot's disgust.
While helping the man, one of the pregnant wives falls off the rig, and the despot fatally runs her over.
Another wife finds the warrior hiding in the rig and consoles him.
At night, the lieutenant and the man drive through a swamp and get stuck in the mud.
They slow the despot's forces with landmines, but one of his allies continues the pursuit in his ATV.
The lieutenant and the man work together to blind the ally and disable his ATV.
Moved by that wife's compassion, the warrior joins the group and helps get the rig moving again.
In the morning, the lieutenant tells the man that her group is escaping to her homeland, the bountiful land where she grew up before being kidnapped and brought to the fortress.
She spots a watchtower of her homeland and identifies herself to the woman at top who summons their matriarchal clan.

The clan recognise the lieutenant as one of their own but inform a devastated lieutenant that her homeland was the now-uninhabitable swamp from the previous night and that only seven of the clan are left.
The group decides to ride across an immense salt flat, hoping to find a new home on the other side.
The man goes his own way.

After seeing a vision of the child he was unable to save, the man catches up with the group and convinces them to return to the fortress since they do not know what lies beyond the salt flat, but do know that the now-undefended fortress has ample water and crops.
The despot intercepts them, and in the ensuing battle, five of the clan are killed, one of the wives is captured, and the lieutenant is severely wounded.
The despot overtakes the rig as they approach the canyon.
While the man fights the despot's son and enforcer, the lieutenant boards the despot's truck to rescue the captured wife, who distracts the despot, allowing the lieutenant to kill him.
The remnants of the group drive the despot's truck back to the fortress, while the warrior sacrifices himself by wrecking the rig to block the canyon behind them, killing the enforcer.
The man transfuses his blood to the lieutenant, saving her life.
Back at the fortress, the people rejoice upon learning of the despot's death.
As the man's companions are lifted to the despot's cliffside fortress, the man and the lieutenant glance at each other before the man disappears into the crowd.
In the near future, humanity faces extinction due to dust storms and widespread crop blights.
The pilot, a widowed former space agency test pilot, works as a farmer and raises his children, a daughter and a son, with his father-in-law.
Following a dust storm, the pilot and the daughter discover that dust patterns in the daughter's room, which she had attributed to a ghost, result from a gravitational anomaly.
The pilot recognizes the patterns as binary code specifying coordinates, which lead him and the daughter to a secret space agency facility headed by a professor.

The professor explains that 48 years earlier, a wormhole appeared near a distant planet, apparently placed there by an unknown intelligence, leading to a system in another galaxy with 12 potentially habitable planets located near a black hole.
Volunteers of an earlier expedition had previously traveled through the wormhole to evaluate the planets, with three reporting back desirable results.
The pilot is enlisted to pilot the ship through the wormhole as part of a mission to colonize a habitable planet with 5,000 frozen embryos and ensure humanity's survival.
Meanwhile, the professor would continue his work on solving a gravity equation whose solution would enable construction of a spacecraft for an exodus from the home planet.
The pilot accepts against the daughter's wishes and promises to return.
When she refuses to see him off, he leaves her his wristwatch to compare their relative time when he returns.
The crew, consisting of the pilot, two robots, and three scientists (one of them the professor's daughter), traverses the wormhole after a two-year voyage to the distant planet.
The pilot, a scientist, and the professor's daughter use a lander to investigate the first volunteer's planet, where time is severely dilated.
They land in knee-high water and find only wreckage from the first volunteer's expedition before a gigantic tidal wave kills the scientist and waterlogs the lander's engines.
By the time they leave the planet, the pilot and the professor's daughter discover that 23 years have elapsed on the ship.

Having enough fuel left for only one of the remaining planets, the pilot and the other scientist decide to go to the second volunteer's planet, despite the professor's daughter's protests, as he is still broadcasting.
En route, they receive messages from the home planet.
The pilot watches the son grow up, marry, and have his first son, who soon passes away, while the adult daughter is now a scientist working on the gravity equation with the professor.

On his deathbed, the professor confesses to the daughter that the ship's crew was never meant to return, since a complete solution to the equation was impossible to obtain without measurements from inside a black hole.
On the second volunteer's planet, they awaken him from cryostasis, and he assures them that colonization is possible, despite the extreme environment.
During a scouting mission, the second volunteer attempts to kill the pilot and reveals that he falsified his data in the hope of being rescued.
He steals the pilot's lander and heads for the ship.
A booby trap set by the second volunteer kills the other scientist, but the professor's daughter rescues the pilot with the other lander and they race back to the ship.
The second volunteer is killed in a failed manual docking operation, badly damaging the ship, but the pilot is able to regain control of the spacecraft through his own docking maneuver.
With insufficient fuel, the pilot and the professor's daughter resort to a slingshot around the black hole, which costs them 51 years due to time dilation.
In the process, the pilot and the first robot detach in their craft to lighten the ship so that the professor's daughter and the second robot may reach the third volunteer's planet.
Falling past the black hole's event horizon, they eject from their craft and find themselves in a tesseract made up of infinite copies of the daughter's bedroom across moments in time.
The pilot deduces that the tesseract was constructed by advanced humans in the far future, and realizes that he had always been the daughter's "ghost".
Using Morse code, he manipulates the second hand of her wristwatch to transmit the data the first robot collected, enabling the daughter to complete the gravity equation's solution.
The tesseract, its purpose fulfilled, collapses, ejecting the pilot and the first robot.
The pilot wakes up on a station orbiting the distant planet.
He reunites with the daughter, now elderly and on her deathbed, who tells him to seek out the professor's daughter.
The pilot and the first robot take a spacecraft to rejoin the professor's daughter and the second robot, who are establishing the human colony on the third volunteer's planet.
On June 6, 1944, soldiers of the army land at the beach during the invasion, suffering heavily from artillery and machine gun fire from the fortified German defenders.
Initially dazed by the ferocity of the defense, a battalion captain.
The captain leads a surviving group up the cliffs to neutralize the coastal defenses firing onto the beach, ensuring the success of the landings.
The war department receives communication that three of four brothers have been killed in action; the last, a paratrooper of an airborne division, is listed as missing.
A general.
The general orders that the paratrooper be found and sent home, to spare his family the loss of all its sons.

The captain is tasked with recovering the paratrooper and assembles a detachment of soldiers to accompany him: a first, second, third, fourth, and fifth soldier, a medic, and an interpreter, who lacks combat experience.
The group tracks the paratrooper to a town, where the third soldier is killed by a German sniper while trying to rescue a young girl.
Mourning their friend, the men grow resentful at being forced to risk their lives for one man.
They later find another paratrooper, but realize he is the wrong man with a similar name.
That evening, the men rest in a chapel, where the captain tells the first soldier that his hands began uncontrollably shaking after he joined the war.
The men travel to a rallying point where the airborne division might be after landing off course, where they find scores of wounded and displaced soldiers.

The medic admonishes the second soldier, the fourth soldier, and the fifth soldier for callously searching through a pile of deceased soldiers' dog tags in front of passing troops, hoping to find the paratrooper's among them and conclude their mission.
Remorseful for ignoring their behavior, the captain shouts for anyone who knows the paratrooper; one soldier tells him that the paratrooper was reassigned to defend a vital bridge in another town.
On the way, the captain decides to neutralize a German gun nest they discover, against the advice of his men, and although they are successful, the medic is killed.
The men prepare to execute a surrendered German soldier in revenge, but the interpreter intervenes, arguing that they should follow the rules of war.
The captain releases the soldier, ordering that he surrender to the next Allied patrol.

Discontented with the mission, the second soldier threatens to desert, leading to a standoff between the men that the captain defuses by revealing his civilian background as a teacher and baseball coach, which he had always refused to disclose.

The captain muses that people often guessed his career before he became a soldier, while his men could not, implying that war has changed him, and worries whether his wife will still recognize him after the war.

In that town, the captain's detachment finds the paratrooper and informs him of their mission, but the paratrooper refuses to abandon his post or his fellow soldiers, believing he does not deserve to go home more than anyone else.
The first soldier convinces the captain that saving the paratrooper might be the only truly decent thing they can accomplish during the war.
The captain takes command of the paratrooper's group as the only officer present and prepares the soldiers for a German assault.
During the battle, the fifth soldier and the first soldier are killed, and the interpreter stands paralyzed with fear as the fourth soldier is stabbed to death.
The released soldier returns and shoots the captain before reinforcements arrive to defeat the Germans.
The interpreter confronts the released soldier, who attempts to surrender again, and kills him.
The interpreter and the second soldier observe as the mortally wounded captain tells the paratrooper to earn the sacrifices made to send him home.
Decades later, the elderly paratrooper and his family visit the captain's grave at the cemetery.
The paratrooper expresses that he remembers the captain's words every day, has lived his life the best he could, and hopes he has earned their sacrifices.
In the north of a country, a priest takes part in an archaeological dig in the ancient ruins of a city.
During the dig, he finds a stone talisman of a winged being that evokes a concerned look on his face.
He then visits an ancient statue of the same being, silently confronting it.
In a city neighborhood, an actress is starring in a film directed by her friend.
The actress, along with her 12-year-old daughter, rents a large house with hired help.
While spending time in the house, the girl discovers a spirit board.
Unaware of traditional superstitions regarding the board, she plays with it alone.
She tells her mother she has made repeated contact with an entity she calls by a nickname.
Meanwhile, another priest, a psychiatrist who counsels university priests, visits his ailing mother in another city.
He later confides to a colleague that he is having a crisis of faith.
The actress hosts a party with the psychiatrist's friend, a priest, who explains the psychiatrist's role as counselor and notes his mother's recent death.
The girl, seemingly unwell, appears and urinates before the actress comforts her.
The girl's bed shakes violently after the actress returns her to it.
Later, the friend consoles the psychiatrist, guilty at not having been with his mother when she died.
The girl's personality becomes violent, and medical tests find no physical cause.
During a house call, the girl exhibits abnormal strength and adult behavior, and speaks in an otherworldly voice.

One night, the actress finds the house empty except for a sleeping girl; the director had been left with her but is found dead at the bottom of a set of public stairs that begin beneath the girl's window.
A detective questions the psychiatrist, confiding that the director's head was turned backward.
The detective tells the actress that the only plausible explanation for the director's death is that he was pushed from the girl's window.
As the detective leaves, a scarred and bloody girl has another violent fit, furiously masturbating with a crucifix, turning her head backward and speaking in the voice of the director.
She is confined to her bedroom and strapped to the bed.
Now convinced that her daughter is possessed, the actress seeks out the psychiatrist, who visits the girl.
The possessed girl claims to be the devil, and vomits into the psychiatrist's face while speaking in tongues.
The demon says it will remain in the girl until she is dead.
The psychiatrist throws holy water onto the girl, causing her to react violently and speak in a bizarre language which he records.
He later admits to the actress that it was tap water, causing him to doubt she is possessed.
He has a linguist analyze the language on the tape, who concludes that it is perfect English being spoken backward.
At night, the actress's assistant calls the psychiatrist to the house, where the words 'help me' appear carved in the girl's stomach from the inside; he concludes that an exorcism is warranted.
His superior grants permission on the condition that an experienced priest lead the ritual.
The priest, having performed an exorcism before, is summoned.
The priest arrives at the house.
As the two priests read from the ritual book, the demon curses them.
The priests rest and the priest, shaking, takes nitroglycerin.
The psychiatrist enters the bedroom where the demon appears as his mother, perturbing the psychiatrist despite his denials.
The priest excuses the psychiatrist and continues the exorcism by himself.
The actress approaches the psychiatrist and asks if the girl will die.
He assures her that she will not and re-enters the room, finding the priest dead from a heart attack while the girl watches and laughs.
Enraged, the psychiatrist beats the possessed girl and demands that the demon take him instead.
The demon rips the medallion of a saint from the psychiatrist's neck and does so, freeing the girl in the process.
Unwilling to let the demon harm the girl, the psychiatrist sacrifices himself by jumping out the window, tumbling down the stone stairs outside to his death.
A man takes a caretaker position to look after a remote hotel in the mountains while it is closed for the winter.
On arrival, the hotel manager informs the caretaker that a previous caretaker killed his wife, two young daughters and himself in the hotel a decade prior.

At home in the city, the caretaker's son has a premonition and seizure; the caretaker's wife tells the doctor about a past incident when the caretaker accidentally dislocated the boy's shoulder during a drunken rage.
The caretaker has been sober ever since.
Before leaving for the seasonal break, the hotel's head chef informs the boy of a telepathic ability the two share, which the chef's grandmother called "shining".
He tells the boy that the hotel also "shines" due to its residual and unpleasant history and warns him to avoid room 237.
A month passes, and the boy starts having frightening visions, including those of the murdered sisters.
Meanwhile, the caretaker's mental health deteriorates; he suffers from writer's block, is prone to violent outbursts, and has dreams of killing his family.
The boy gets lured to room 237 by unseen forces, and the wife later finds him with signs of physical trauma, for which she blames the caretaker.
The caretaker defiantly sulks in the ballroom, where a ghostly bartender entices him back to drinking.
The wife tells him that the boy was attacked by a "crazy woman" in room 237.
The caretaker investigates and encounters a hideous female ghost in the bathroom, but tells the wife he saw nothing.
He blames the boy for inflicting the bruises on himself and reacts angrily when the wife suggests leaving the hotel.
The boy enters a trance and telepathically contacts the chef.
Returning to the ballroom, the caretaker finds it filled with ghostly figures, including a waiter, who urges the caretaker to "correct" his wife and child.
The wife finds the caretaker's manuscript written with nothing but countless repetitions of the proverb "All work and no play makes the caretaker a dull boy".

When the caretaker threatens her life, the wife knocks him unconscious with a baseball bat and locks him in the kitchen pantry, but she and the boy are snowed in—the caretaker previously sabotaged the hotel's two-way radio and snowcat.
Back in their private apartment, the boy begins to chant, from a murmur, "red rum" more and more loudly ("red RUM") and writes it out in lipstick on the bathroom door.
The wife sees the word in the mirror which shows that it spells MURDER in reverse, and she panics.
The waiter frees the caretaker, who goes after the wife and the boy with an axe.
Taking shelter in the bathroom, the wife fights off the caretaker with a knife when he tries to break through the door; the boy escapes out the bathroom window.
The chef, having flown back to the state from his winter home in another state, reaches the hotel by snowcat.
The caretaker ambushes and murders him with the axe, then pursues the boy into an expansive hedge maze on the hotel grounds.

With trepidation the wife runs through the hotel looking for the boy, encountering the hotel's ghosts, the chef's bloody corpse, and a vision of cascading blood from an elevator similar to the boy's premonition.
The boy carefully backtracks in the snow to mislead the caretaker and hides behind a snowdrift.
While the caretaker rushes ahead without a trail to follow and becomes lost, the boy exits the maze and is found by the wife.
The two depart the hotel in the chef's snowcat, leaving the caretaker to freeze to death in the maze.
Meanwhile, a photograph in the hotel hallway pictures a man, by all appearances the caretaker, standing amidst a crowd of party revelers from July 4, 1921.
In 1955, the teenage protagonist becomes enamored by the criminal life and mob presence in a working class Italian American neighborhood in the city.
He begins working for a local caporegime and his associates, an Irish American truck hijacker and gangster, and a fellow juvenile delinquent predisposed to violence.
The protagonist begins as a fence for the hijacker, gradually working his way up to more serious crimes.
In 1965, the protagonist starts dating a Jewish American woman who is initially confused by the protagonist's criminal activities.
She is soon seduced by the protagonist's glamorous lifestyle and marries him despite the disapproval of her parents.
The protagonist, the delinquent, and the hijacker manage to excel in carjacking and stealing cargo trucks from the airport, and eventually, they commit a robbery against an airline in 1967.
On June 11, 1970, a made man in a crime family, who was recently released from prison, incessantly insults the delinquent at a nightclub owned by the protagonist.
In response, the delinquent and the hijacker brutally beat him to his apparent death.

Realizing that the unsanctioned murder of a made man will invite retribution, the hijacker, the protagonist and the delinquent bury the body upstate, stabbing and fatally shooting him when he is discovered to be alive.
Six months later, the hijacker learns that the burial site is slated for development, prompting them to exhume and relocate the decaying corpse.
In 1974, the wife harasses the protagonist's mistress and threatens the protagonist at gunpoint.
The protagonist moves in with the mistress, but the caporegime insists that he return to the wife after collecting a debt from a gambler in another city with the hijacker.
The hijacker and the protagonist are arrested after being turned in by the gambler's sister, a federal typist, and they receive ten-year prison sentences.
To support his family on the outside, the protagonist has the wife smuggle in drugs from out of town, which he sells to fellow inmates.
In 1978, the protagonist is paroled and expands his cocaine business with the hijacker and the delinquent against the caporegime's orders.
The hijacker organizes a crew to raid an airline's vault at the airport, stealing six million dollars in cash and jewelry.
After some members purchase expensive items against the hijacker's orders and the getaway truck is found by police, he has most of the crew killed.
Only the protagonist and the delinquent are spared, as the protagonist is making him money through his out-of-town connection and the delinquent is about to become a made man.
However, the delinquent is killed when he arrives at the bogus initiation ceremony in 1979 in retribution for murdering the made man, much to the hijacker's dismay and anger.
By 1980, the protagonist has become a nervous wreck due to heavy cocaine use.
He sets up another drug deal with his out-of-town associates but is arrested by narcotics agents and incarcerated.
After bailing him out, the wife explains that she flushed $60,000 worth of cocaine down the toilet to prevent federal agents from finding it during their raid, leaving the family penniless.

Feeling betrayed by the protagonist's drug dealing and realizing that he is a liability, the caporegime gives him $3,200 out of pity and ends their association - which revokes the protagonist's protection from the hijacker, and makes him fair game.
The protagonist meets the hijacker at a diner and is asked to travel to a hit assignment, but the request makes him suspicious.
The protagonist concludes that the hijacker plans to have him killed and decides to finally become an informant and enroll with his family in the witness protection program.

The protagonist gives sufficient testimony and evidence in court to have the caporegime and the hijacker convicted, and moves to a neighborhood in an undisclosed location, in accordance with the witness protection program.
The protagonist describes his unhappiness by leaving his exciting and turbulent gangster life, feeling condemned to live a boring, average life as a "schnook".

In the city, a former marine and war veteran takes a job as a night-shift taxi driver to cope with his chronic insomnia and loneliness, frequently visiting adult movie theaters on his breaks, and keeping a diary in which he consciously attempts to include aphorisms such as "you're only as healthy as you feel".
He becomes disgusted with the crime and urban decay that he witnesses regularly in the city and dreams about getting "the scum off the streets", recording these dreams in his diary.
His narration throughout the film is largely conveyed through voice-over excerpts from his diary, which reveal his deteriorating mental state and deepening alienation from society.
The veteran becomes infatuated with a campaign worker for a senator, who is running for president.
The veteran enters the campaign office where she works and asks her to join him for coffee, to which she agrees.
The campaign worker agrees to go on a second date with him, during which he takes her to an adult movie theater, which she leaves immediately.
He attempts to reconcile with her, but fails.
The rejection further deepens his isolation and contributes to his increasingly erratic behavior.
Enraged, he storms into the campaign office where she works and berates her before being kicked out of the office.
Experiencing an existential crisis and seeing various acts of prostitution throughout the city, the veteran confides in a fellow taxi driver about his violent thoughts.
However, the fellow driver dismisses them and assures him that he will be fine.
Despite this reassurance, the veteran remains emotionally unmoored, unable to articulate the depth of his psychological distress.
To find an outlet for his rage, the veteran follows an intense physical training regimen.
He gets in contact with a black market gun dealer and buys four handguns.
At home, the veteran practices drawing his new weapons, going as far as creating a quick-draw firearm hidden in one of the sleeves in his coat.
He begins attending the senator's rallies to scope out his security.
He also writes a threatening letter to the senator, further indicating his intent to act against him.
One night, the veteran shoots a man attempting to rob a convenience store run by his friend, leaving before the cops arrive as the convenience store owner proceeds to beat the non-responsive robber.
In his trips around the city, the veteran regularly encounters a 12-year-old child prostitute.
Tricking her pimp and abusive lover into thinking that he wants to solicit her, the veteran meets with her in private and tries to persuade her to stop prostituting herself.
The veteran shaves his hair into a mohawk and attends a public rally where he plans to assassinate the senator.
However, security agents see the veteran putting his hand inside his jacket and approach him, which escalates to a chase.
The veteran escapes pursuit and makes it back to his home undetected.
That evening, the veteran drives to the brothel where the girl works to kill the pimp.
He enters the building and shoots the pimp and one of the girl's clients, a mafioso.
The veteran is shot several times but manages to kill the two men.
He fights with the bouncer, whom he manages to stab through the hand with his knife and kill with a gunshot to the head.
The veteran attempts to die by suicide, but has no bullets.
Severely injured, he slumps on a couch next to the sobbing girl.
As the police respond to the scene, the delirious veteran mimics shooting himself in the head with his bloody finger.
The veteran goes into a coma due to his injuries, but he is hailed by the press as a heroic vigilante who saved the girl and is not prosecuted for the homicides.
He also receives a handwritten letter from the girl's parents in another city, who thank him for saving their daughter, revealing that she's safe and attending school once more.
After recovering, the veteran returns to work, where he encounters the campaign worker as a fare.
The campaign worker tells him that she followed his story in the newspapers.
The veteran drops her off at her home but declines to take her money, driving off with a smile.
He briefly becomes agitated after noticing something in his rearview mirror, but continues driving into the night.
